notes:
UNITS CORRECTION 2026-10-04 (parent agent; arithmetic 49.24/8=6.155 confirms it): price_usd is PER GPU-HOUR, not per node. The prior label said 'per 8-GPU node per HOUR'. The stored number was always right, so the defect was invisible to review and to validate.py -- it is exactly the failure price_basis exists to prevent, and CoreWeave is a reference rental point in docs/08-cost-per-token.md. The most USEFUL price structure in the slice, because CoreWeave publishes all three columns - on-demand, spot, and a third 'Inference Single GPU' rate - which lets you read the market rather than guess at it. On on-demand H100 ($6.155/GPU-hr) CoreWeave sits between AWS p5 ($6.88) and the neoclouds. On SPOT H100 ($19.71/8 = $2.46/GPU-hr) it is the cheapest published H100 hour anywhere in this slice, ~64% under AWS on-demand and ~29% under even Runpod's in-stock Pod rate. The third column is the one to understand before quoting: 'Pricing based on GPUs is exclusively applicable to the CoreWeave inference platform customers' with the footnote 'contact your account executive' - so the $6.16 'Inference Single GPU' H100 number is gated to their inference platform, NOT a bare-GPU rate you can walk in and buy, and it happens to equal the on-demand per-GPU figure anyway. Also note regional asymmetry: spot is CHEAPER in Europe than North America for H100 ($19.51 vs $19.71), H200 ($20.64 vs $20.93) and A100 ($9.51 vs $9.65) - if you are EU-based, Europe is the cheaper spot market, the reverse of the usual intuition. Region-restricted deployments carry a stated 1.5x premium. The GB200 NVL72 line is the outlier worth noting: $42.00/h for 72 Blackwell GPUs is $0.58 per GPU-hour, which is not comparable to the 8-GPU node pricing and suggests rack-scale pricing is a different economic model entirely - and it is quoted for Europe too, which is unusual for a rack-scale SKU. Spot is published per region and changes continuously.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
